Division 2 is more dangerous than Division 1
Division 1 can have an ignitible mixture in normal operation, including frequent maintenance; Division 2 only under abnormal conditions
They depend only on the gas group
explanation: Division 1 covers places where a flammable mixture can show up during normal work, including releases from frequent repairs. Division 2 covers places where it is likely only if something goes wrong, short of a catastrophe. Source: NFPA 497-2027, 5.3.1.1 to 5.3.1.3 and 5.3.2.

question: In the Zone system, what does Zone 0 mean under NFPA 497?
choices: An ignitible mixture is present all the time or for long periods
The area is unclassified
A mixture appears only during abnormal conditions
Combustible dust is present
explanation: Zone 0 is the most severe gas zone, where the mixture is present continuously or for long stretches. Zone and Division labels are not interchangeable. Source: NFPA 497-2027, 5.4.1.

question: What should the size of a classified area be based on under NFPA 497?
choices: A fixed 10 ft radius around every valve
The color of the piping
The NEC article number
The material, its release conditions and the site's real ventilation and layout, not a stock diagram
explanation: Extent depends on things like vapor density, LFL, temperature, pressure, release size and ventilation. Barriers, wind and room shape matter too. Ask operations and maintenance about leaks and routine work. Source: NFPA 497-2027, 5.6.1 to 5.6.4 and 5.9.2.1 to 5.9.2.4.

question: Under NFPA 499, combustible dust clouds form during normal operation or frequent maintenance. Which classification does that support?
choices: Class I, Division 2
Zone 20 or 21, or Class II, Division 1
Class III
Unclassified
explanation: Dust clouds in normal operation or frequent maintenance point to Class II, Division 1 in the Division system, or Zone 20 or 21. Rare releases of some dust groups may fall to Division 2 or Zone 22. Source: NFPA 499-2027, 6.2.3.2 to 6.2.3.5.

question: During a site walk you see a dust layer on a motor. Does NFPA 499 give a dust thickness that passes or fails the motor electrically?
choices: Yes. Over 1/8 in. fails the insulation test
No. Layer depth is an input to the area classification review, not an electrical test limit
Yes. Any dust fails
Yes. Over 1 in. requires a hipot
explanation: NFPA 499 has the team ask how thick layers get and how fast dust builds up, as part of classifying the area. Housekeeping and tight equipment help limit the classified area. It is not a pass/fail number for the equipment. Source: NFPA 499-2027, 6.6.2.2 and 6.8.6.

question: Under NFPA 70E-2027 120.6, how is the absence-of-voltage test done on a low-voltage circuit?
choices: Test one phase to ground at the panel and assume the rest
Use the panel voltmeter
Check that the breaker handle is in the off position
At every work location, check every phase and circuit part line to line and line to ground, proving the tester on a live source before and after
explanation: The tester has to be rated for the job. Prove it on a live source you trust, test every phase at every work point both line to line and line to ground, then prove the tester again. Source: NFPA 70E-2027, 120.6(7).

question: On a 13.8 kV system, may a noncontact capacitive tester replace contact testing under NFPA 70E-2027?
choices: Yes, over 1000 V an appropriately rated noncontact tester may check each phase, but it can't prove absolute absence of voltage
No, never
Yes, on any system of any voltage
Only if it is used at the remote end
explanation: Exception 2 allows noncontact capacitive instruments above 1000 V. The note explains that these devices have a minimum operating voltage, so they show no detectable voltage, not zero voltage. Source: NFPA 70E-2027, 120.6(7) Exception 2.

question: On a current-driven circuit, the absence-of-voltage test alone doesn't prove the circuit is de-energized. What does NFPA 70E-2027 require?
choices: Nothing more; a zero-voltage reading is enough
Apply grounds and skip testing
Additional test methods, such as testing for absence of current
Repeat the voltage test three times
explanation: Exception 3 says when a voltage test can't settle the question, use more methods. The informational example is checking for absence of current on circuits driven by a current source. Source: NFPA 70E-2027, 120.6(7) Exception 3.

question: Under NFPA 70E-2027, an energized work permit calls for shock or arc-flash PPE. Who else must be there?
choices: Nobody, if the worker is qualified
A second worker inside the restricted approach boundary
At least one person trained in emergency response, standing beyond whichever is bigger: the limited approach boundary or the arc-flash boundary
The AHJ
explanation: The 2027 edition requires at least one extra person with the emergency response training of 110.4(C)(1). That person stays beyond the bigger of the two boundaries, limited approach or arc flash. Source: NFPA 70E-2027, 130.2(A)(2).

question: A new double-ended 480 V switchboard is ready for energization from either utility source. Mechanical inspections are complete, but no one has confirmed bus phasing from both sources. What should you require before the lineup is accepted?
choices: Perform phasing checks from each source and confirm that the bus phasing matches the intended design before the sources can be paralleled or transferred
Skip phasing on a double-ended board; nameplate voltage is enough
Megger each bus section and treat a passing insulation-resistance test as proof of correct phasing
Energize one source only and assume the second source is already in phase
explanation: On double-ended or dual-source switchgear, ATS requires phasing checks so that bus phasing from each source is correct and agrees with the design. A clean insulation-resistance test does not prove phase rotation or phase correspondence between sources. Accepting the lineup without that check leaves a paralleling or transfer error waiting to happen. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025, 7.1.1.B.13 and 7.1.1.D.13.

question: You are proving the current wiring in a new switchgear lineup. The plan is to inject into each CT secondary so that at least 1.0 A flows in the secondary wiring and then read the current only at the first relay in each section. Is that enough?
choices: Yes. If 1.0 A is seen at the first relay, the rest of the circuit can be assumed correct
Secondary injection is not used for this check; only a 50 A primary shot at the bus is accepted
Any convenient secondary current is fine, and you only need to confirm that the wiring is continuous with a buzzer
No. Inject so that at least 1.0 A flows in the secondary circuit, and verify the correct current magnitude at each device in that circuit
explanation: ATS current-injection tests that cover every current path in the lineup call for a secondary current of at least 1.0 A and a check that the correct magnitude appears at each device. Proving one relay does not prove a tap, a shorted winding, or a swapped lead farther down the circuit. Optional primary injection uses the same 1.0 A secondary criterion. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025, 7.1.1.B.10 and 7.1.1.D.10.

question: A double-ended lineup has automatic control-power transfer relays. After CPT tests, a technician reports that secondary voltage is correct and wants to close the job without operating the transfer relays. What is the right call?
choices: Correct CPT secondary voltage is enough; transfer relays are only a maintenance item
Require the control-power transfer relays to be operated and shown to perform as designed before you accept the lineup
Transfer relays are proven by the bus dielectric test
Leave the transfer relays to the owner to try after energization
explanation: ATS treats control-power transformer tests and control-transfer-relay function as separate checks. Secondary voltage can be right while a transfer relay fails to switch sources, leaving a dead control bus on loss of one CPT. The transfer relays must perform as designed before acceptance. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025, 7.1.1.B.7.5 and 7.1.1.D.8.5.

question: You are the person in charge of locking out a lineup that has two sources, two crews, and a shift change mid-job. What does NFPA 70E require of a complex lockout/tagout?
choices: A written plan of execution that names the person in charge, who has overall responsibility
Each qualified person may run a simple lockout on their own cubicle with no common plan
A tag on the main breaker is enough if everyone on the crew has been briefed
Only the host employer's safety manager may place locks; testers do not take part
explanation: NFPA 70E treats simple and complex lockout as two forms of hazardous-energy control. On a simple lockout the qualified person is in charge. On a complex lockout the person in charge has overall responsibility, and the procedure requires a written plan of execution that identifies that person. Multiple sources, more than one crew, or a job that spans a shift are the usual reasons a lockout is treated as complex. Source: NFPA 70E-2024, 120.3(H) and 120.5.

question: A crew lead wants to isolate a motor with the stop pushbutton and hang a tag on the start station, leaving the disconnect shut. What is your call under NFPA 70E?
choices: Accept it if the tag says Do Not Operate and the stop button is taped down
Accept it for jobs shorter than one shift
Reject it. Locks and tags go on the circuit disconnecting means, not on control devices such as pushbuttons
Accept it when the motor is less than 50 hp
explanation: Locks and tags are installed only on circuit disconnecting means. Control devices such as pushbuttons or selector switches are not the primary isolating device. The disconnect has to be opened and locked, and every person who could be exposed, directly or indirectly, is involved in the procedure. Source: NFPA 70E-2024, 120.3(A) and 120.3(E).

question: How often does NFPA 70E require a qualified person to audit the lockout/tagout program and procedures, and what must that audit include?
choices: Once every five years, by reviewing paperwork only
Only after an incident, and a tabletop review is enough
At intervals not exceeding one year, and it must cover at least one lockout/tagout in progress
Monthly, by the same person who wrote the procedure
explanation: The lockout/tagout program and the procedures in 120.2 through 120.6 are audited by a qualified person at intervals not to exceed one year. The audit has to cover at least one lockout in progress and is meant to catch problems in the program, the training, and how workers actually carry out the procedure. The employer is responsible for those audits. Source: NFPA 70E-2024, 110.3(L)(3) and 120.2(B).

question: Your testing company is coming onto a plant site as a contractor. Under NFPA 70E, what information must the host and the outside testing contractor share with each other?
choices: The host must tell the contractor about known hazards related to the work; the contractor must brief its people on those hazards and on the host's safety rules, and must tell the host about unique hazards the contractor brings
Only the host's written safety manual needs to be handed over; no discussion is required
The contractor is solely responsible, so the host has no duty to mention site hazards
A single signed waiver replaces any information exchange
explanation: The host employer informs contract employers of known hazards related to the contractor's work that the contractor might not recognize, and of information the contractor needs for its assessments. The contract employer makes sure its people are informed of those hazards and follow the host's safety-related work rules, and advises the host of unique hazards the contractor's work creates. Where the host knows of hazards related to the contractor's work, the meeting is documented. Source: NFPA 70E-2024, 110.5.

question: Before a crew starts work on a lineup that may have exposed energized parts, what must the job safety plan include under NFPA 70E?
choices: Only a toolbox talk about PPE, with no documented assessments
Only the incident-energy number from the last five-year study, with no shock assessment
A generic permit that does not address this equipment
A shock assessment that follows 130.4 and an arc-flash assessment that follows 130.5, plus a description of the job and the tasks
explanation: Before starting each job, a job safety plan and a job briefing are required. The plan has to describe the job and the individual tasks, include a shock risk assessment per 130.4 when there is a shock hazard, and include an arc-flash risk assessment per 130.5. Approving those assessments is a senior-technician duty on the Level IV outline. Source: NFPA 70E-2024, 110.3(I) and 110.3(H).

question: A supervisor wants to solve an arc-flash problem on a 480 V lineup by buying higher-rated clothing and leaving the equipment and work methods unchanged. What does NFPA 70E's hierarchy of risk control require you to consider first?
choices: PPE is the preferred first control because it is the fastest to implement
Start at the top of the hierarchy (elimination, then substitution, then engineering controls) and use PPE only after those higher-order measures are addressed
Awareness signs alone satisfy the hierarchy if they are posted on the door
Once clothing is selected from the PPE-category tables, no other controls are considered
explanation: The risk-assessment procedure requires that preventive and protective controls be applied following the hierarchy of risk control. Higher-order controls such as elimination, substitution, and engineering are applied at the source. Administrative controls and PPE come later and do not replace a decision about whether the hazard can be reduced or removed. Source: NFPA 70E-2024, 110.3(H)(3).

question: A qualified technician is only going to take voltage readings and check a relay, staying on the test procedures in Chapter 1 and using the right PPE. Is an energized electrical work permit required?
choices: Yes. Any approach to energized parts requires a signed permit, with no exceptions
No. Testing, troubleshooting, or voltage measuring by a qualified person using appropriate safe work practices and PPE is an exemption
No only if the incident energy is below 1.2 cal/cm2
Yes unless the plant manager verbally waives the permit
explanation: An energized electrical work permit is required for energized work when 110.2(B) applies, but 130.2(C) lists exemptions. Testing, troubleshooting, or voltage measuring is one of them, provided a qualified person uses appropriate safe work practices and PPE. Thermography, ultrasound, or visual inspections, access and egress, and housekeeping can also be exempt when the restricted approach boundary is not crossed. Source: NFPA 70E-2024, 130.2(C).

question: You manage rubber insulating gloves for a test crew. What does NFPA 70E require for in-service gloves?
choices: A visual check once a year is enough if the gloves look clean
Electrical retests are required only after a known puncture
New gloves may go into service without any prior electrical test
Inspect and air-test them before each day's use, and electrically retest issued gloves at intervals not exceeding six months
explanation: Insulating gloves are checked for damage at the start of each workday and given an air test as part of that check. Rubber insulating equipment also gets periodic electrical tests, and gloves that have been issued for service must be retested electrically at least every six months. New insulating equipment stays out of service if its last electrical test is more than a year old. Source: NFPA 70E-2024, 130.7(C)(7)(c) and Table 130.7(C)(7)(b).

question: The arc-flash labels on a switchgear lineup are several years old, and no one can show when the supporting data was last checked. What does NFPA 70E require?
choices: The data behind the labels must be checked for accuracy at least once every five years, and a label is updated if that check finds a change that makes it inaccurate
Labels never need review once they are applied
A review is required only after a personal injury
Any label applied before the current edition must be replaced immediately, even if the system has not changed
explanation: The method of calculating and the data that support the label information are documented. That data is checked for accuracy at least once every five years. If the review finds a change that makes the label inaccurate, the label is updated. The owner of the equipment is responsible for documentation, installation, and maintenance of the marked label. An older label can remain if it met the edition in effect when it was applied and the system has not changed in a way that makes it inaccurate. Source: NFPA 70E-2024, 130.5(H).

question: An incident-energy study used a relay's time-current curve but ignored the fact that the breaker's last maintenance was years overdue and the trip unit is sticky. What does NFPA 70E require of the incident energy analysis?
choices: Maintenance condition is ignored; only the manufacturer's published clearing time is used
Only bolted-fault current matters; clearing time is not part of the analysis
The calculation must account for the overcurrent device's operating characteristics, how long it takes to clear, and whether the device is in proper condition of maintenance
Condition of maintenance is considered only for outdoor equipment
explanation: If incident energy is calculated rather than taken from a PPE-category table, the exposure is based on the working distance of the employee's face and chest from a prospective arc source for the specific task. The calculation must account for the overcurrent device's operating characteristics, how long it takes to clear, and whether the device is in proper condition of maintenance. A device that may not operate as designed cannot be assumed to clear in the published time. Source: NFPA 70E-2024, 130.5(G).
